messages.content: What is the function of ATP synthase in mitochondria?

message.content:
ATP synthase—also called F₁F₀‑ATPase—is the key enzyme that produces most of the cellular energy in eukaryotic cells. In mitochondria it sits embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and uses the electrochemical proton gradient generated during electron transport to drive synthesis of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) from adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and inorganic phosphate (Pi).

**How it works**

| Component | Location & role |
|-----------|----------------|
| **Fo sector** | Embedded in the inner membrane; forms a proton channel. Proton movement through Fo turns a central stalk. |
| **F1 sector** | Extends into the matrix; contains catalytic sites where ADP + Pi → ATP occurs. Rotation of the central stalk drives conformational changes at each β subunit, cycling between “open,” “loose” and “tight” states that bind substrates, catalyze bond formation, and release product. |

As electrons pass along the respiratory chain, protons are pumped out of the matrix creating an electrochemical potential (ΔpH + membrane potential). Protons flowing back down this gradient through Fo rotate the rotor, which mechanically powers the synthetic activity of F1. This coupling makes ATP synthase one of nature’s most efficient molecular motors.

In short, ATP synthase converts the stored energy of a proton motive force into chemical energy in the form of ATP—the universal currency of cellular work.
